title: Jenkins Declarative Pipelines
description: Write robust Jenkins pipelines using the declarative syntax with stages, steps, and environment management.

data.text: A **Jenkins Pipeline** is a code-based representation of your CI/CD workflow. Pipelines are defined in a `Jenkinsfile` that lives alongside your application code in version control. This approach — Infrastructure as Code for your build process — makes your pipeline reviewable, versioned, and consistent across environments.
There are two syntaxes: **Declarative Pipeline** (recommended, structured) and **Scripted Pipeline** (older, Groovy-based). This lesson focuses on Declarative Pipeline.

Specifies where to run stages (any available agent)

Container for the sequence of build stages
A named phase of the pipeline with its own steps

terms.definition: A named phase of the pipeline (e.g., build, test, deploy) containing one or more steps.
The smallest unit of work — a single command, action, or script invocation.
Specifies where (which node or container) the pipeline or stage executes.
Actions that run after the pipeline completes, based on success, failure, or always.
A conditional directive that controls whether a stage executes.

data.text: The `agent` directive tells Jenkins where to run the pipeline. `agent any` runs on any available node. You can also use `agent none` at the top level and specify agents per-stage, or target specific labeled agents.

data.title: Agent per stage
data.content: Run some stages on a specific node label and others anywhere.

data.caption: Declarative pipeline stages flow from build through test to deploy and post-actions.

data.text: You can make stages conditional with `when` directives and run them in parallel to speed up builds.

data.title: Parallel and conditional stages
data.content: Run tests in parallel and deploy only on the main branch.

data.title: Post-build actions
data.text: Always define a post-build section with cleanup steps. Use `always { cleanWs() }` to clean the workspace, and notify the team on `success` or `failure`.

items: `BUILD_NUMBER` — Unique number for this pipeline run.
`BUILD_URL` — Full URL to the build results.
`GIT_COMMIT` — The commit hash the build is based on.
`JOB_NAME` — Full name of the Jenkins job.

cards.title: Declarative
cards.description: Structured syntax with clear sections; recommended for most teams.

cards.title: Scripted
cards.description: Full Groovy-based syntax for complex custom logic.

data.text: For Git projects, use a **Multibranch Pipeline** job. Jenkins scans the repository, finds branches with a `Jenkinsfile`, and creates a separate pipeline job for each one. This lets you run different pipelines for feature branches, staging, and main.

data.title: Write a multistage pipeline
data.description: Create a Jenkinsfile for a simple application.
steps: Choose a simple app (e.g., a Node.js or Python project).
Write a `Jenkinsfile` with Checkout, Build, Test, and Deploy stages.
Add environment variables for version and image name.
Add a post section that sends a notification on failure.
Set up a Multibranch Pipeline job in Jenkins pointing at your repo.
Push a change and watch the pipeline execute.
data.expectedOutcome: A working multistage pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys your app.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Pipelines as code (Jenkinsfile) are versioned, reviewable, and consistent.
Structure pipelines with agent, environment, stages, and post sections.
Use `when` for conditionals and `parallel` for faster test runs.
Multibranch Pipeline jobs automatically discover and build branches.
Always clean up workspaces and notify the team on pipeline status.
data.takeaway: Declarative pipelines give you a readable, maintainable way to automate your entire CI/CD workflow.
